# Ontological Exhaustion

I had fun writing my most recent newsletter, which went viral. It was based on this [[20nzf7p7kdhqjer2jfrfj29exf | blyg post]]. But I’m a bit puzzled about why a lot of people reacted like it was a major aha idea. The basic idea is not that deep, though some of the historical arguments are new in the AI debate. So why are so many people reacting like it is?

I think the reason is there’s a dual phenomenon to [[3bsgmfd5d6540eyxsq7e796fp0 | Ontological Inventiveness]] that explains it. *Ontological exhaustion* is when there is so much change happening that the rate at which you have to become aware of and adopt new categories to think with overwhelms you.

It’s orthogonal to language acquisition. Being immersed in a new language is overwhelming, but because most languages are approximate ontological equivalents at the 101 level (there’s a word for *cat* in most languages), you don’t actually have to learn many new concepts. You just have to learn new words for old ones, alongside a few novel sentence patterns. So you feel like you’re drowning for a while but at some point you experience a phase transition and start “thinking” in the new language.

A new reality otoh requires you to use a familiar language in unfamiliar ways. You have to make up a lot of new nouns or recode old ones. It’s like landing on a new continent with completely different wildlife. You have to invent or borrow words like “kangaroo” and repurpose words like “robin” to refer to different objects (there’s American robin is a different family and unrelated to the European one, despite both having red breasts). This is overwhelming in a different way. I do think a similar phase shift happens when you can start thinking in a new ontology.

Since I proposed ontological inventiveness as an element of leadership, especially of thought leadership. But ontological exhaustion means in times of extreme change you have to do more than invent categories and terms. You have to model usage in language, which requires a community of speakers using the evolved language in steadily expanding, useful ways. So it’s a collective action challenge rather than a leadership challenge. You can’t race the new stuff and win, at least initially, but you can make the new way of talking steadily more usable. You won’t get rid of FUD but you’ll experience less FUD than other groups.
